content: 1. A study by Ersek (2009) found no significant association between third-trimester exercise and postnatal depressive symptoms after adjusting for maternal age and marital status. The absolute difference was 4 fewer cases per 1,000 (ranging from 2 fewer to 6 fewer), but the quality of evidence was rated as very low. 2. Data from the Danish National Birth Cohort (Strom 2009) could not be included in the meta-analysis. All odds ratios (ORs) were adjusted for maternal age, parity, pre-pregnancy BMI, alcohol intake, smoking, occupation, education, home ownership, marital status, social support, and history of previous depression. 3. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) by Satyapriya (2013) comparing yoga (n=51) with non-yoga antenatal exercises (n=45) demonstrated an improvement in state anxiety symptoms with yoga but not with other antenatal exercises. The quality of evidence was rated as low. 4. Beddoe (2009) reported that a seven-week mindfulness-based yoga intervention did not reduce state anxiety symptoms, regardless of whether the intervention was introduced in the second or third trimester of pregnancy (n=16). The quality of evidence was rated as low. 5. Another RCT by Satyapriya (2013) showed that yoga improved trait anxiety symptoms compared to non-yoga antenatal exercises. However, the quality of evidence was rated as low. 6. Beddoe (2009) also found that a seven-week mindfulness-based yoga intervention reduced trait anxiety symptoms when introduced in the third trimester but not in the second trimester (n=16). The quality of evidence was rated as low. 7. Two systematic reviews (Davenport 2018 and 2019) were identified to support the 2019 Canadian Guideline for Physical Activity Throughout Pregnancy. These reviews addressed the relationship between physical activity and fetal health outcomes. 8. Two RCTs (Baciuk et al., 2009; de Oliveira et al., 2012) reported no association between prenatal exercise and low birth weight (<2500 g). Additional data from three studies (Kasawara et al., 2013; Barakat et al., 2016; Ussher et al., 2015) also found no significant association. The quality of evidence was rated as low. 9. Among pregnant women with overweight or obesity, six RCTs (n=863) found no significant difference in the risk of small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants between physical activity intervention groups and controls. The quality of evidence was rated as moderate. 10. Two studies (de Oliveira et al., 2012; Oostdam et al., 2012) reported no association between prenatal exercise and high birth weight (>4000 g). Additional data from four studies (Kasawara et al., 2013; Barakat et al., 2013; Tomic et al., 2013) supported these findings. The quality of evidence was rated as moderate. 11. One study (Cavalcante et al., 2009) found no association between prenatal exercise and preterm birth. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. 12. Among pregnant women with overweight or obesity, six RCTs (n=737) found no significant difference in the risk of preterm birth between physical activity intervention groups and controls. The quality of evidence was rated as very low. 13. A cohort study by Madsen (2007) involving 92,671 women found a progressive increase in the odds of miscarriage with increasing exercise volume. However, secondary analyses including only women interviewed about exercise habits prior to miscarriage showed different results. The quality of evidence was rated as very low.
